message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for highly parallel tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each core is powerful, with deep pipelines, large caches, complex control logic. | Many thousands of simpler cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups. Each core is lightweight; the focus is on throughput rather than single‑thread latency. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with sophisticated branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution, speculative execution. | Very simple instruction set, often fixed‑function pipelines optimized for vector operations. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated memory controllers, support for virtual memory, page tables, TLBs. | Smaller per‑core caches, rely heavily on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR). Memory access patterns are usually predictable (coalesced). |
| **Parallelism** | Thread‑level parallelism: a few threads run concurrently, each thread may have its own pipeline. | Data‑parallelism: thousands of threads execute the same instruction on different data elements simultaneously. |
| **Latency vs Throughput** | Optimized for low latency – quick response to individual instructions. | Optimized for high throughput – many operations completed per cycle, but higher latency per operation. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks, branching, I/O, operating system services, database queries, web servers. | Tasks that can be expressed as the same operation applied to many data items: image/video processing, neural network inference/training, scientific simulations, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Programming Model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded code written in C/C++, Java, etc., compiled to native binaries. | Parallel programming models like CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX compute shaders, Metal, Vulkan compute, or higher‑level frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch). |
| **Power Efficiency** | Power‑efficient for general tasks; scaling power with performance is complex due to branch mispredictions, cache misses, etc. | Power‑efficient for throughput‑heavy workloads; many cores share resources, so idle cores consume little power. |
| **Cost & Size** | Cheaper per core, smaller die area per core, more flexible. | More expensive per core, larger die area, but cost per FLOP (floating‑point operation) is lower for massive parallel workloads. |

### Why the difference matters

* **Branching** – CPUs handle unpredictable branches well; GPUs suffer when branches diverge because all threads in a warp (group) must execute the same instruction path.
* **Memory Access Patterns** – CPUs benefit from random access and caching; GPUs need coalesced, sequential memory accesses to achieve peak bandwidth.
* **Precision** – GPUs historically favored lower precision (FP16, INT8) for speed; modern GPUs support FP32/FP64 and mixed‑precision for AI workloads.

In practice, most systems use both: the CPU orchestrates overall program flow, while the GPU accelerates compute‑intensive kernels. This synergy is why GPUs are now common in gaming rigs, data centers, and even consumer laptops.
